issues.legal_issue: Statutory vesting of a public street in a municipality does not transfer ownership of the underlying site or soil to the municipality.
material_facts: The disputed land adjoined the footpath and road and formed part of the public street.
The State owned the land before the municipal legislation applied.
The municipality purported to lease the land to the respondent, who built a house on it.
issues.conclusion: The land fell within the statutory definition of a street, but the municipality acquired only the street qua street and did not acquire the State’s ownership of the underlying land.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(23) and 116(g) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, a public street vests in a municipality as a street, not as absolute property; the vesting does not transfer the owner’s rights in the site or soil. The Court followed Municipal Board, Mangalur v. Sri Mahadeoji Maharaj, which approved the reasoning in S. Sundaram Ayyar v. The Municipal Council of Madura and the Secretary of State for India in Council.

predicates.public_street_land: The land formed part of a public street, including land within the defined boundary of property abutting the road.
predicates.state_owned_underlying_land: The State owned the underlying land before it vested in the municipality as a street.
predicates.municipal_vesting_of_street: The street vested in the municipality for its statutory management and control.

issues.definition: When land owned by the State forms part of a public street that vests in a municipality, the municipality holds the street for its street purpose while the State retains ownership of the underlying land.

issues.legal_issue: The State may seek to recover public-street land from an illegal occupant when the street is put to a use other than a street.
material_facts: The State owned the underlying land, although the street vested in the municipality for street purposes.
The respondent occupied the land and built a house under a purported lease granted by the municipality.
The respondent’s earlier injunction suit against the municipality had been decreed, but the State was not a party to that suit.
The State brought an action seeking removal of the construction and possession of the land.
issues.conclusion: Because the municipality’s interest was limited to the street qua street and the land was put to another use, the State was entitled to maintain an action to evict the respondent and recover possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 116(g) and 118 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, the municipality’s statutory interest in a street is for its management and control as a street; that interest ends when the street ceases to be used as a highway. The underlying owner may intervene when the street is put to another use and may evict an illegal occupant. The Court applied Municipal Board, Mangalur v. Sri Mahadeoji Maharaj, which followed the reasoning in S. Sundaram Ayyar v. The Municipal Council of Madura and the Secretary of State for India in Council.

rule.if: state_eviction_action and public_street_land and state_owned_underlying_land and municipal_vesting_of_street and street_put_to_nonstreet_use and occupant_lacks_valid_right_against_state

predicates.state_eviction_action: The State brought an action to remove an occupant or construction from the land and recover possession.
predicates.public_street_land: The land formed part of a public street.
predicates.state_owned_underlying_land: The State owned the underlying land notwithstanding its use as a public street.
predicates.municipal_vesting_of_street: The municipality held the street for its management and control as a street.
predicates.street_put_to_nonstreet_use: The land was diverted from use as a street to another use.
predicates.occupant_lacks_valid_right_against_state: The occupant had no valid right to occupy the land enforceable against the State.

issues.definition: When the State seeks possession of land it owns beneath a public street, the street has been put to another use, and the occupant lacks a valid right against the State, the State may recover possession from that occupant.
